title: The capital stack and loan-to-cost
summary: Every development is paid for by layers of money that stand in a line, from the safest lender at the bottom to the owner's own cash at the top. Loan-to-cost tells you how much of the bill the lender is carrying and how much is left for equity to fund.
body:
A project's total cost is funded by a stack of layers: senior debt, mezzanine debt, preferred equity and common equity. Loan-to-cost measures how much of that stack is borrowed, and the rest is the equity cushion that protects the lenders.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, think of the total development cost as one bill, and the capital stack as the list of people who pay it. Each layer puts in money on different terms, and the terms follow one simple trade: the layer that gets paid first takes the least risk and accepts the lowest return.

  • Senior debt sits at the bottom. It is usually a construction loan secured by a first mortgage on the land and the building. It is paid first and charges the lowest interest rate.
  • Mezzanine debt sits on top of the senior loan. It is still a loan with a fixed interest rate, but it is usually secured by a pledge of the ownership interests rather than by the property itself, so it is paid only after the senior lender. It charges a higher rate.
  • Preferred equity is ownership money with a priority claim. It is not a loan, but it gets its money back, plus a fixed preferred return, before common equity sees anything.
  • Common equity is the top of the stack: the developer and the investors. It is paid last, it absorbs the first loss, and it keeps whatever profit is left over. That last claim is why it can earn the highest return.

The headline ratio is loan-to-cost.

Loan-to-cost (percent) = loan amount (dollars) ÷ total development cost (dollars) × 100

Lenders look at it two ways. Senior loan-to-cost uses only the senior loan. Combined, or "last-dollar", loan-to-cost adds the mezzanine loan, because it tells you how deep into the stack borrowed money reaches before the owners' money starts. Equity is simply what is left:

Equity required (dollars) = total cost − all debt

A worked example

A hypothetical apartment project has a total development cost of 20 million dollars, including land, hard costs, soft costs and interest carry.

  1. The senior lender offers 60 percent loan-to-cost. Senior loan = 0.60 × 20 million = 12 million dollars.
  2. A mezzanine lender adds 15 percent of cost. Mezzanine = 0.15 × 20 million = 3 million dollars. Combined debt = 15 million dollars, so combined loan-to-cost = 15 ÷ 20 = 75 percent.
  3. That leaves 20 − 15 = 5 million dollars of equity.
  4. A preferred equity investor puts in 2 million dollars. The developer and partners put in the last 3 million dollars as common equity.
LayerDollarsShare of costPaid
Common equity3 million15 percentLast
Preferred equity2 million10 percentThird
Mezzanine debt3 million15 percentSecond
Senior debt12 million60 percentFirst
Total20 million100 percent

Always check that the layers add back to total cost. Here 12 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 20. If they do not add up, there is a funding gap, and a funding gap discovered halfway through construction is how projects stall.

Two practical points. First, equity usually goes in first: lenders typically require the owners to spend their money before the loan funds a single draw, so the cushion exists from day one. Second, the ratio a lender offers is a business decision that varies by lender, market and project, not a fixed rule.

Why does any of this matter to an owner? Because every layer of debt that replaces equity raises the return on the equity that remains, and also thins the cushion between the project and a loss. Tomorrow you will see exactly who loses what when the value falls.

This is education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

Try each one before you open the answer. Round figures, hypothetical deals.

Problem 1

A project costs 10 million dollars. The senior lender will lend at 65 percent loan-to-cost, and there is no mezzanine. How large is the loan, how much equity is required, and what share of cost is equity?

Problem 2

A project costs 30 million dollars. The senior loan is 18 million dollars and a mezzanine loan adds 4.5 million dollars. Work out the senior loan-to-cost, the combined loan-to-cost and the equity required. Then the mezzanine lender asks to increase to 6 million dollars: what happens to combined loan-to-cost and to equity?

Problem 3

You show a senior lender a stack with 25 percent equity. What would a lender ask about that equity before agreeing to fund? Name at least three questions.

The roommate question

On the power grid you do not rely on one barrier against an outage: there are protection relays, reserves and operator action in layers. How is a capital stack like layered protection, and which layer of the stack plays the role of the "first thing to give way"?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Loan = 0.65 × 10 million = 6.5 million dollars.
  2. Equity = 10 − 6.5 = 3.5 million dollars.
  3. Equity share = 3.5 ÷ 10 = 35 percent, which is simply 100 − 65.

The usual error: applying the percentage to the land price or the hard cost instead of the total development cost. Loan-to-cost is measured against the whole bill.

Rule: loan plus equity always equals total cost.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Senior loan-to-cost = 18 ÷ 30 = 60 percent.
  2. Combined debt = 18 + 4.5 = 22.5 million; combined loan-to-cost = 22.5 ÷ 30 = 75 percent.
  3. Equity = 30 − 22.5 = 7.5 million dollars, or 25 percent.
  4. With 6 million of mezzanine: combined debt = 24 million, combined loan-to-cost = 24 ÷ 30 = 80 percent, and equity falls to 6 million dollars, or 20 percent.

The usual error: quoting only the senior loan-to-cost and calling the deal "60 percent leveraged". The equity cushion is set by all the debt above and below it, so the combined figure is the one that tells you how thin the cushion really is.

Rule: judge leverage by the last dollar of debt, not the first.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
Typical lender questions:

  • Is it cash, or is it land value? Lenders often discount equity that is credited land value above what was paid for it.
  • Where does it come from? Lenders want to see the source, and they dislike equity that is itself borrowed, because then it is not really a cushion.
  • When does it go in? Usually equity must be spent before the first loan draw.
  • Who covers overruns? If costs rise, does more equity come in, and who guarantees that?
  • Does the sponsor have real money at risk? A developer with little of their own cash in the deal has less reason to stay and fix problems.

The usual error: treating equity as a number on a page. To a lender it is a cushion, and a cushion only works if it is real, committed and in first.

Rule: equity protects the lender only if it is real cash, at risk, and in first.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
Grid protection works in layers so that a single failure is absorbed by the outer layers before it reaches the customer. The capital stack works the same way in reverse: losses arrive at the top of the stack first. Common equity is the first thing to give way, then preferred equity, then mezzanine, and the senior lender is the last to feel anything, much like the load that is protected by every other layer. The thicker the equity, the bigger the disturbance the stack can absorb before the senior lender is touched.

Rule: equity is the first line of defence for every layer beneath it.

rule: Loan-to-cost is debt divided by total cost; the equity cushion is everything left over, and it takes the first loss.

title: Loss order: who gets paid first
summary: When a project is sold or refinanced, the cash pays each layer of the stack in order from the bottom up. That means losses start at the top, so the owner's equity is wiped out before a lender loses a dollar.
body:
The capital stack is paid from the bottom up and loses from the top down. If you know the order, you can say in seconds who is whole and who is wiped out at any sale price.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, yesterday you met the four layers. Today the question is what happens when the money comes back, at a sale or a refinance, and there is less of it than was put in.

The answer is a strict queue, often called the waterfall or priority of payments. Cash flows down the queue: the senior lender is repaid in full first; whatever is left goes to the mezzanine lender until it is repaid; whatever is left after that goes to preferred equity; and common equity gets the remainder, if any. Nobody further down the queue receives a cent until the layer in front of them is paid in full.

Turn that around and you get the loss order. If proceeds are short, the shortfall lands on the top layer first. Common equity loses everything before preferred equity loses anything, and so on down.

The formulas are simple. For each layer, in order:

Paid to this layer = the smaller of (what it is owed) and (cash remaining)

Loss to this layer = what it is owed − what it is paid

And a useful check: total losses = total cost − proceeds, when proceeds are below cost.

A worked example

Same hypothetical project as yesterday: 20 million dollars of cost, funded by 12 million senior, 3 million mezzanine, 2 million preferred equity and 3 million common equity. The market softens and the finished project sells for 16 million dollars. To keep the arithmetic clean we will ignore interest, fees and selling costs, which in real life make losses worse.

  1. Senior is owed 12 million and 16 million is available. Senior is paid 12 million in full. Cash left: 4 million.
  2. Mezzanine is owed 3 million and 4 million is available. Mezzanine is paid 3 million in full. Cash left: 1 million.
  3. Preferred equity is owed 2 million but only 1 million is left. It is paid 1 million and loses 1 million, which is half its money.
  4. Common equity is owed 3 million and nothing is left. It loses all 3 million.
LayerPut inPaid backLoss
Senior debt12 million12 million0
Mezzanine3 million3 million0
Preferred equity2 million1 million1 million
Common equity3 million03 million

Check: total losses are 1 + 3 = 4 million, and cost minus proceeds is 20 − 16 = 4 million. They match.

Notice the shape of the result. The value fell by 20 percent, yet the common equity lost 100 percent. That is leverage working in reverse, and it is the single most important thing to understand about being the owner.

How far can value fall before a layer is hurt?

Each layer is safe until proceeds fall below the top of its layer, measured from the bottom. Senior is safe down to 12 million, a 40 percent fall from cost. Mezzanine is safe down to 15 million, a 25 percent fall. Preferred equity is safe down to 17 million, a 15 percent fall. Common equity starts losing on the first dollar below 20 million. This "attachment point" is exactly how lenders think about their cushion.

Real loan documents add detail, such as intercreditor agreements that set out what the mezzanine lender may do in a default. This lesson is education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

Ignore interest, fees and selling costs in every problem.

Problem 1

A project costs 10 million dollars: 6 million senior, 1.5 million mezzanine and 2.5 million common equity. It sells for 8 million dollars. What does each layer get back, and what percentage does common equity lose?

Problem 2

A project costs 50 million dollars: 30 million senior, 7.5 million mezzanine, 5 million preferred equity and 7.5 million common equity. It sells for 36 million dollars. Who is paid what, and who loses what? Then: by what percentage can the value fall below cost before the senior lender loses a single dollar?

Problem 3

A mezzanine lender is considering the deal in Problem 2. What would that lender ask the sponsor and the senior lender before committing?

The roommate question

In grid operations, when supply is short, load is shed in a set priority order, and critical loads are protected last. How is that like the loss order of the capital stack?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Senior is owed 6 million; 8 million available. Paid 6 million. Left: 2 million.
  2. Mezzanine is owed 1.5 million; 2 million available. Paid 1.5 million. Left: 0.5 million.
  3. Common equity is owed 2.5 million; paid 0.5 million, so it loses 2 million.
  4. Percentage lost = 2 ÷ 2.5 = 80 percent.

Check: losses 2 million = cost 10 − proceeds 8.

The usual error: spreading the 2 million loss across everyone in proportion to what they put in. The stack is a queue, not a shared pot.

Rule: pay from the bottom, lose from the top.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Senior: owed 30, paid 30 million. Left: 6 million.
  2. Mezzanine: owed 7.5, only 6 left. Paid 6 million, loses 1.5 million, which is 20 percent.
  3. Preferred equity: nothing left. Loses all 5 million.
  4. Common equity: loses all 7.5 million.

Check: 1.5 + 5 + 7.5 = 14 million = 50 − 36.

Senior cushion: senior is whole until proceeds drop below 30 million. From a cost of 50 million that is a fall of 20 million, and 20 ÷ 50 = 40 percent. That is simply 100 percent minus the 60 percent senior loan-to-cost.

The usual error: forgetting that preferred equity is still equity. It sits above the mezzanine loan, so it is wiped out before the mezzanine lender loses its last dollar.

Rule: a layer's cushion is everything stacked above it.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• Where is my attachment point? The mezzanine lender is hurt once value falls below 37.5 million, only 25 percent under cost, so it wants to know how realistic that is.
  • What does the intercreditor agreement say? Can it step in and take control of the ownership if the deal goes wrong, and does it get notice of a senior default in time to cure it?
  • How much real equity is above me? The 12.5 million of preferred and common equity is its cushion, so it asks whether that is cash and whether it goes in first.
  • Who funds cost overruns? Every dollar of overrun that is borrowed rather than funded by equity eats its cushion.
  • Any guarantees? Mezzanine lenders often ask the sponsor for completion or carve-out guarantees.

The usual error: thinking a lender only cares about the property's value. A mezzanine lender cares just as much about what sits above it and what rights it has when things go wrong.

Rule: a lender's real question is how much loss stands between it and its money.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
Under-frequency load shedding drops blocks of load in a fixed order so that the system survives and essential loads, such as hospitals, stay on. The capital stack sheds losses the same way: common equity is shed first, then preferred equity, then mezzanine, and the senior loan is the protected load kept on to the end. In both cases the order is agreed before the event, so nobody negotiates in the middle of a crisis.

Rule: priority is decided before the shortfall, not during it.

rule: Cash pays the stack from the bottom up, so losses hit common equity first and the senior lender last.

title: A two-tier equity waterfall with a preferred return
summary: Inside the equity layer, investors and the sponsor split profits through a waterfall: first everyone gets their money back plus a preferred return, then the remaining profit is split with an extra share to the sponsor. Knowing the tiers lets you see exactly when the sponsor's promote starts to pay.
body:
An equity waterfall decides how the owners share cash among themselves. Tier one returns everyone's capital plus a preferred return; tier two splits what is left, with a bigger slice, the promote, going to the sponsor.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, the capital stack told you how lenders and owners rank against each other. Now look inside the common equity. It usually has two kinds of owner: investors, often called limited partners, who put in most of the cash, and the sponsor or developer, often called the general partner, who finds and runs the deal and puts in a smaller amount.

The sponsor wants to be rewarded for creating profit. The investors want to be protected until the deal has at least earned a fair minimum. A two-tier waterfall does both.

  1. Tier one, return of capital plus preferred return. All cash goes to the equity partners in proportion to what they put in, until each has received its capital back plus a preferred return, often around 8 percent a year. That rate is a negotiated term, not a standard.
  2. Tier two, the split. Everything above tier one is split on a different ratio that favours the sponsor, for example 70 percent to investors and 30 percent to the sponsor, even if the sponsor only put in 10 percent of the money. The sponsor's extra share is called the promote or carried interest.

For a simple preferred return, which is what we will use:

Preferred return (dollars) = equity (dollars) × pref rate (percent a year) × years

Tier one total = equity + preferred return

Tier two pool = cash distributed − tier one total (zero if negative)

Real agreements often compound the preferred return and add more tiers or a catch-up. We keep it to two simple tiers so the logic is clear.

A worked example

A hypothetical project needs 10 million dollars of common equity: investors put in 9 million (90 percent) and the sponsor 1 million (10 percent). The preferred return is 8 percent a year, simple, and the project is sold after 2 years, leaving 14 million dollars for the equity after all debt is repaid.

  1. Preferred return = 10 million × 0.08 × 2 = 1.6 million dollars.
  2. Tier one total = 10 + 1.6 = 11.6 million. Split 90 to 10: investors 10.44 million, sponsor 1.16 million.
  3. Tier two pool = 14 − 11.6 = 2.4 million. Split 70 to 30: investors 1.68 million, sponsor 0.72 million.
  4. Investors receive 10.44 + 1.68 = 12.12 million on 9 million in: a profit of 3.12 million, or about 34.7 percent over two years.
  5. Sponsor receives 1.16 + 0.72 = 1.88 million on 1 million in: a profit of 0.88 million, or 88 percent over two years.

Check: 12.12 + 1.88 = 14 million. Every dollar is accounted for.

InvestorsSponsorTotal
Tier one10.44 million1.16 million11.6 million
Tier two1.68 million0.72 million2.4 million
Total received12.12 million1.88 million14 million

See the shape again. The sponsor's percentage return is far higher than the investors', but only because the deal cleared the preferred return. If the deal does badly, the promote is worth nothing and the sponsor earns the same rate as everybody else. That is the point: the promote pays for outperformance, not for showing up.

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

Investors 90 percent and sponsor 10 percent of the equity, an 8 percent simple preferred return, and a 70 to 30 split in tier two, unless the problem says otherwise.

Problem 1

Equity is 5 million dollars. The project is sold after 1 year and 6 million dollars is distributed to the equity. How much does each party receive, and what is each party's percentage profit?

Problem 2

Equity is 10 million dollars, held 2 years, but only 11 million dollars is distributed. How much does each party receive? Does the sponsor earn any promote, and how much more cash would the deal need before tier two receives its first dollar?

Problem 3

You show the senior lender a waterfall in which you, as sponsor, could earn 88 percent on your cash. What would a lender ask about it, and why does the promote not comfort the lender at all?

The roommate question

On the grid, a reserve is held back before anything else is committed, and only the margin above it is available for other uses. How is a preferred return like that reserve?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Preferred return = 5 million × 0.08 × 1 = 0.4 million.
  2. Tier one = 5 + 0.4 = 5.4 million. Investors 90 percent = 4.86 million; sponsor 10 percent = 0.54 million.
  3. Tier two pool = 6 − 5.4 = 0.6 million. Investors 70 percent = 0.42 million; sponsor 30 percent = 0.18 million.
  4. Investors receive 4.86 + 0.42 = 5.28 million; profit 0.78 million on 4.5 million = about 17.3 percent.
  5. Sponsor receives 0.54 + 0.18 = 0.72 million; profit 0.22 million on 0.5 million = 44 percent.

Check: 5.28 + 0.72 = 6 million.

The usual error: applying the 70 to 30 split to the whole 6 million. Tier two only gets what is left after capital and the preferred return.

Rule: fill tier one completely before splitting anything on the promote.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Preferred return = 10 million × 0.08 × 2 = 1.6 million. Tier one needs 11.6 million.
  2. Only 11 million is available, so all of it stays in tier one, split 90 to 10: investors 9.9 million, sponsor 1.1 million.
  3. Each earns 10 percent over two years (0.9 on 9, and 0.1 on 1), which is short of the 16 percent the preferred return promised.
  4. The sponsor earns no promote. Tier two starts only once cash passes 11.6 million, so the deal needs another 0.6 million dollars.

The usual error: assuming the sponsor always gets 30 percent of profit. The promote only exists above the preferred return; below it, the sponsor is just another investor.

Rule: no preferred return, no promote.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• How much of your own cash is in, and when? The lender cares about the sponsor's cash equity, not projected upside.
  • Do the investors' rights affect us? Can investors remove the sponsor, and what happens to guarantees and management if they do?
  • Is any distribution allowed before our loan is repaid? Lenders usually restrict cash going out to equity while the loan is outstanding.
  • Are the investors able to fund a capital call if costs run over?

The promote does not comfort the lender because it is paid after the loan, out of profit the lender never shares. A large promote can even worry a lender if the sponsor has little cash at risk, since the sponsor then has much to gain and little to lose.

The usual error: presenting an attractive equity return to a lender as if it strengthens the loan. The lender's return is capped at its interest; only the cushion protects it.

Rule: lenders are reassured by cash at risk, not by upside.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
An operating reserve is set aside first, and only the capacity above it can be dispatched for other purposes. A preferred return works the same way: the investors' capital and their minimum return are "held back" first, and only the margin above that line, tier two, is available to reward the sponsor. If the margin never appears, the reserve still protects the investors.

Rule: the promote is paid only from the margin above the reserve line.

rule: Fill tier one with capital plus the preferred return first; only the cash above it is split, and only that split pays the sponsor's promote.
